summary:
Amapá stands under Brazil's national framework, and no state-level deviation affecting a visitor is documented in the sources. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14-1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015. Legal gender change has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018, and gender-marker change proceeds by self-determination.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, docketed as ADO 26 and MI 4733, carrying imprisonment of one to five years and fines. That ruling is the operative basis on which homophobia and transphobia are treated as criminal conduct anywhere in the country, including Amapá.

Documents remain the area where a visitor may see divergence. There is no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender as precedent. Non-binary birth-certificate practice varies from state to state, so the entry a person obtains in Amapá is not guaranteed to match what another state's registry will accept. Trans voters may also register under their lived name and identity before their documents are updated.

Enforcement does not track the statutory text evenly. The country retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, and an expat legal guide updated in April 2026 records that enforcement of the protections is uneven in practice. Major cities such as São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Brasília, Belo Horizonte, Curitiba and Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. For Amapá this translates into the national position carried with a remote-interior discount on services and enforcement, and no state-specific hostility on record. The national survey's per-state table carries a 2022-dated entry recording progress in Amapá on recognition documents.
tangentialFactors:
Brazil's LGBTIQ legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, so the durability of the protective statutes is contested at national level rather than settled. The same legal package is described by an expat legal guide as among the most progressive LGBTQ+ protections in Latin America on paper, which sets the comparison point against which Amapá's practice should be read.

The gap between statute and street is the recurring pattern: the country's violence rates against sexual and gender minorities remain among the highest recorded anywhere, with trans people bearing the greatest share, and the divergence between well-resourced metropolitan legal infrastructure and thinner provision in interior towns is the specific mechanism a visitor in Amapá is likely to notice.
localsOnly:
Residents of Amapá share the full national suite of rights: joint adoption since 2010 with full rights from 2015, name and gender-marker change without surgery, and criminal liability for homophobia and transphobia on the same footing as racism. Civil registrars may record non-binary or unspecified gender entries, and the 6 May 2025 Superior Court of Justice ruling gives neutral-gender rectification standing as precedent.

Political visibility at resident level is documented. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022, and more than 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections. Trans voters in Amapá may register to vote under their lived name and identity before their identity documents are updated.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports Amapá-specific enforcement data, state-level court decisions, or recorded incidents of violence against trans people in the state, so the assessment of local practice rests on the national pattern rather than on evidence gathered in Amapá itself.

The position of Amapá's civil registry on non-binary or neutral-gender entries is unresolved: the sources establish that practice varies state by state and that such entries have been possible nationally since 2020, but they do not state which option, if any, Amapá's registrars currently offer.

The outcome of the repeal pressure reported in the conservative Congress is unresolved in the sources, as is any question of whether Resolution 348/366 detention-placement rules have been applied in Amapá's custodial facilities; neither is sourced here.
